To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) antibiotic use after free tissue transfer for head and neck reconstruction is common, with 90% of patients receiving a minimum of 5 days of antibiotics, 2) antibiotic use after reconstruction is not associated with a decrease in postoperative infection rates, and 3) antibiotic use after head and neck reconstruction may be associated with an increased risk of Clostridium difficile infection.

(i) short course antibiotic use is as effective as long course antibiotic use in preventing infection after head and neck reconstruction; and (ii) the use of short course antibiotic use results in a lower incidence of antibiotic associated diarrhea and a higher patient satisfaction rate.

1) The short-course antibiotic protocol is as safe as long course protocol in patients undergoing FTM surgery, 2) The short course protocol is associated with a shorter hospital stay, 3) There is a significant reduction in cost of care for patients treated with the short-course antibiotic protocol.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of antibiotics in free tissue transfer for head and neck reconstruction.
the study of the effects of the use of antibiotics in the postoperative period of patients with free tissue reconstruction of head and neck defects.
the use of antibiotics after free flap surgery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of prophylactic antibiotics for the prevention of surgical site infection (SSI) in free flap reconstruction of head and neck defects is not supported by the current evidence.
there are no clear indications to support the use of long course antibiotic prophylaxis after free flap reconstruction.
there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the use of antibiotics in the immediate post-operative phase after free tissue reconstruction in the head and neck.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
short-course antibiotic prophylaxis is as effective as long-course antibiotic prophylysis for free flap reconstruction of head and neck defects.
we found that there was not a significant difference in outcomes between short course and long course antibiotics after free tissue reconstruction of head and neck defects.

the use of antibiotics in the immediate post-operative phase of free flap reconstruction of the head and neck can be safely limited to a short course of antibiotics (3 days) with no increase in infection or flap loss.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be more judicious in our use of antibiotics after free flap reconstruction in the head and neck, especially in the era of increasing antibiotic resistance.
there is a significant difference in the number of antibiotic days prescribed after free tissue transfer in the head and neck.
short-course antibiotics are just as good as long-course antibiotics in preventing surgical site infections in head and neck reconstruction.
